name: Triangle from Back
description: Master Triangle from Back in BJJ. Complete guide with safety protocols, setup, execution. Success rates: Beginner 35%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
The Triangle from Back is an advanced blood choke that represents a sophisticated evolution of traditional back control submissions. This technique combines the positional dominance of back control with the mechanical efficiency of the triangle choke, creating a submission that attacks the carotid arteries while maintaining superior position. Unlike the standard rear naked choke, the triangle from back uses leg configuration to create the choking pressure, freeing the hands for positional control and defense nullification.

This submission is particularly effective when the opponent successfully defends the traditional rear naked choke by protecting their neck with their hands or maintaining proper chin position. By transitioning to the triangle configuration, you can bypass many common rear naked choke defenses while simultaneously threatening to return to traditional back attacks. The technique requires exceptional flexibility, timing, and positional awareness, making it a hallmark of advanced no-gi grappling.

The triangle from back also serves as a critical component of modern back attack systems, creating dilemmas where defending one submission opens pathways to others. When properly integrated into a systematic approach to back control, this submission significantly increases your finishing rate from the most dominant position in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate upon release, but repeated unconsciousness can cause cumulative damage

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from improper leg positioning
Trachea compression if triangle is misaligned

safety_considerations.application_speed: EXTREMELY SLOW - 5-7 seconds minimum progression from setup to full pressure
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on your leg or body
Any rapid repeated motion indicating distress
Loss of resistance or going limp (IMMEDIATE RELEASE)
release_protocol: Immediately open triangle legs and separate knees
Release all upper body grips and back control
Monitor breathing and consciousness for 30-60 seconds
If partner is unconscious, elevate legs and call for medical assistance
training_restrictions: Never apply full pressure during initial learning phases
Never use competition speed or intensity in training
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with both hands
Never hold submission after tap signal
Never practice on partners with known neck or cardiovascular issues without medical clearance

key_principles: Maintain back control throughout the transition - never sacrifice positional dominance for submission attempt
Angle your body perpendicular to opponent's spine to create proper triangle geometry
Lock triangle on same side as your choking arm to maximize compression
Use your free hand to control opponent's arm and prevent defensive framing
Apply pressure progressively through hip extension and leg squeeze, never explosive jerking motions
Keep your own posture compact to prevent opponent from rolling or escaping back control
Coordinate upper body control with lower body finishing mechanics for complete submission system
setup_requirements: Established back control with hooks in or body triangle already secured
Opponent defending rear naked choke effectively (chin down, hands protecting neck)
Sufficient flexibility to bring your leg over opponent's shoulder while maintaining back control
Control of at least one of opponent's arms to prevent defensive frames
Ability to create perpendicular angle without losing back position
Understanding of which side triangle to apply based on opponent's arm position

execution_steps.description: Begin from standard back control with both hooks in or body triangle secured. Establish seat belt grip (one arm over shoulder, one under armpit) and ensure your chest is tight to opponent's back. Your goal is complete positional dominance before attempting the triangle transition.

execution_steps.action: Bait and assess rear naked choke defense
execution_steps.description: Attempt a traditional rear naked choke setup by bringing your choking arm across opponent's throat. Observe their defensive reaction - most will tuck their chin hard and grab your choking arm with both hands. This defensive commitment creates the opening for triangle transition.

execution_steps.action: Trap defensive arm on choking side
execution_steps.description: With your non-choking hand, swim over the top and grab opponent's wrist or forearm on the same side as your choking arm. Pull this arm tightly across their body, isolating it. This trapped arm will become part of the triangle choke structure.

execution_steps.action: Create perpendicular angle and remove bottom hook
execution_steps.description: Slide your body toward the side where you've trapped the arm, creating a 90-degree angle to opponent's spine. Remove your bottom hook on the same side, preparing to bring your leg over their shoulder. Maintain top hook and upper body control throughout this transition.

execution_steps.action: Thread leg over shoulder into triangle position
execution_steps.description: Bring your bottom leg over opponent's shoulder on the side where you've trapped their arm. Your calf should rest across their throat while your foot reaches toward your opposite hip. Maintain perpendicular angle - your body should form a T-shape with theirs.

execution_steps.action: Lock triangle and establish figure-four configuration
execution_steps.description: Bring your opposite leg over your ankle to lock the triangle. Your locked legs should create a figure-four around opponent's neck and their own trapped arm. Ensure the bony part of your shin is across their carotid artery on the non-trapped side.

Pull opponent's head down with your choking arm while simultaneously pulling your knees together and extending your hips. The squeeze should come from your entire leg structure, not just calf pressure. Angle your body to increase the perpendicular angle if needed.

execution_steps.action: Maintain control and secure tap or transition
execution_steps.description: Keep your upper body control throughout the finish. If opponent defends successfully by posturing or hand fighting, be prepared to transition back to rear naked choke or other back attacks. Never fully commit to triangle if it sacrifices back control completely.
execution_steps.timing: Hold until tap or defensive escape requires transition

opponent_defense_patterns.defense: Grabbing your ankle to prevent triangle lock completion
opponent_defense_patterns.your_adjustment: Use your free hand to break their grip while simultaneously using your locking leg to kick through their grip. Alternatively, threaten armbar on the grabbing arm to force them to release.

opponent_defense_patterns.defense: Turning into you to alleviate triangle pressure and escape back control
opponent_defense_patterns.your_adjustment: Use your top hook and upper body control to prevent rotation. If they commit to turning, transition to mounted triangle or traditional front triangle position.

opponent_defense_patterns.defense: Posturing up and creating space between their neck and your shin
opponent_defense_patterns.your_adjustment: Pull their head down forcefully with your choking arm while extending your hips. Use your free hand to control their far shoulder and prevent posturing.

opponent_defense_patterns.defense: Hand fighting to create frames and alleviate pressure
opponent_defense_patterns.your_adjustment: Control their free arm with your non-choking hand. If they use both hands to defend, their neck becomes exposed - immediately transition back to rear naked choke. The triangle creates a dilemma where defending it opens other attacks.

common_errors.error: Losing back control entirely during triangle transition
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes to neutral or advantageous position, negating all positional work
common_errors.correction: Maintain at least one hook and upper body control throughout transition. If you can't secure triangle while keeping back control, abandon the attempt and return to standard back attacks.

common_errors.error: Applying triangle with wrong leg (crossing over opposite shoulder from trapped arm)
common_errors.consequence: Triangle geometry fails, no choking pressure achieved, opponent can easily defend or escape
common_errors.correction: Always bring your leg over the shoulder on the SAME side as the trapped arm. The triangle should incorporate their arm into the choke structure.

common_errors.error: Using only calf squeeze without hip extension
common_errors.consequence: Ineffective choke that relies on pain rather than blood flow restriction, easy to defend
common_errors.correction: The finishing pressure comes from pulling knees together WHILE extending hips. Think of it as making your legs straighter while simultaneously closing the triangle.

common_errors.error: Failing to create perpendicular angle to opponent's body
common_errors.consequence: Poor triangle geometry, minimal carotid compression, opponent can defend with posture
common_errors.correction: Your torso should form a T or L shape with opponent's spine. Slide your entire body to the side to create this angle before locking the triangle.

common_errors.error: Applying explosive, jerking motion to finish the choke
common_errors.consequence: High risk of neck injury, trachea damage, or loss of consciousness without tap opportunity
common_errors.correction: SLOW, progressive pressure over 5-7 seconds minimum. The choke should tighten gradually, giving partner ample opportunity to recognize pressure and tap.

common_errors.error: Continuing to squeeze after opponent taps or goes limp
common_errors.consequence: Severe injury risk including brain damage from prolonged blood restriction
common_errors.correction: Immediately release all pressure upon ANY tap signal. If opponent goes limp without tapping, release instantly and begin recovery protocol.

variations_and_setups.variation_name: Triangle from Body Triangle Back Control
variations_and_setups.description: When already in body triangle configuration, transition directly to triangle choke by opening the body triangle and threading your leg over the shoulder. This variation is faster and maintains more control throughout.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have body triangle established and opponent is defending neck effectively

variations_and_setups.description: From gift wrap back control where opponent's arm is already isolated, transition to triangle is cleaner as one arm is pre-trapped. Simply remove bottom hook and bring leg over shoulder on trapped arm side.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you've secured gift wrap and opponent is blocking rear naked choke attempts

variations_and_setups.description: When opponent turtles to escape back control, maintain one hook and thread your opposite leg over their far shoulder. Lock triangle in inverted position, then roll them to complete.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent successfully turtles to escape traditional back control

variations_and_setups.description: If opponent begins turning into you during triangle setup from back, follow their rotation to mounted triangle position. This salvages the submission while adapting to their defensive movement.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent rotates toward you while defending the initial triangle setup

knowledge_assessment.question: What anatomical structures does the triangle from back attack, and how does the choking mechanism differ from air chokes?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The triangle from back attacks the carotid arteries on both sides of the neck, restricting blood flow to the brain rather than cutting off air supply. Your shin compresses one carotid while their trapped arm compresses the other side against your thigh. This blood choke causes unconsciousness in 8-12 seconds under full pressure, compared to air chokes which take longer and are more uncomfortable. The blood choke mechanism is why progressive pressure application is essential for safety.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent starts to posture up during the triangle finish - what grip and hip adjustments secure the tap?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately pull their head down with your choking arm while simultaneously extending your hips forward and pulling your knees together. Use your free hand to control their far shoulder, preventing the posture. If they continue fighting posture, increase hip extension to close the angle between your body and theirs. The combination of head control pulling down and hip extension pushing forward creates an inescapable compression that defeats posturing attempts.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the clear indicators that your triangle is properly locked and the finish is imminent?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Key indicators include: opponent's face changing color (reddening or becoming pale), their resistance weakening noticeably, hands becoming less active in defense, body tension decreasing, and sometimes a slight tremor or softening in their frame. You'll feel the carotid pulse against your leg slow or become irregular. When you observe these signs, the submission is working correctly - maintain steady pressure without increasing force and expect the tap within seconds.

knowledge_assessment.question: What control must be established before you can safely attempt the triangle finish from back?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Before finishing, ensure: the triangle figure-four is completely locked with no gap between your ankle and the back of your knee, your choking arm controls their head angle, at least one hook or your remaining leg maintains some hip control, their trapped arm is genuinely incorporated into the choke structure (not floating free), and your perpendicular angle is established. Rushing to finish without these controls leads to escape opportunities and wasted energy.

knowledge_assessment.question: At what point during the triangle from back does your opponent reach the 'point of no escape' where defense becomes nearly impossible?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The point of no escape occurs when the figure-four lock is fully secured with your ankle deep behind your knee, your body has achieved perpendicular angle to their spine, and you've begun hip extension with the head pulled down. Once these three elements align, traditional defenses like posturing or hand fighting become mechanically ineffective. The opponent's only remaining option is explosive rotation toward you, which should be anticipated and countered with upper body control.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the most common finishing errors that result in losing the triangle from back, and how do you correct them mid-submission?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Common finishing errors include: losing perpendicular angle (correct by sliding your hips further to the side), allowing the trapped arm to slip out (re-trap immediately with your choking hand), squeezing with calves only without hip extension (extend hips while pulling knees together), and losing head control (re-grip their head with your choking arm). Mid-submission corrections must be made decisively - if multiple elements fail simultaneously, consider resetting to basic back control rather than forcing an ineffective finish.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you adjust your grip and squeeze angle when your opponent attempts to two-on-one fight your locking leg?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When opponent grabs your locking leg with both hands, this creates a submission dilemma. First, their neck becomes exposed - consider transitioning immediately to rear naked choke. If you want to finish the triangle, use your free hand to attack their grip while simultaneously extending your hips to increase pressure. You can also threaten armbar on the reaching arms by beginning to rotate your body. The key insight is that defending your leg with both hands means they've abandoned neck defense.

knowledge_assessment.question: What immediate actions must you take if your opponent goes limp before tapping during the triangle from back?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately open your legs completely by separating your knees and unlocking the figure-four. Release all upper body grips and roll opponent to their side in recovery position. Check for breathing and responsiveness. Elevate their legs slightly to restore blood flow to the brain. If unconscious, they typically regain consciousness within 10-20 seconds - do not shake them or apply stimulation. Call for medical assistance if they don't respond within 30 seconds. This represents a training failure - review why tap signals were missed.

knowledge_assessment.question: What competition finishing strategies maximize your tap rate when opponent is actively defending the triangle from back?
knowledge_assessment.answer: In competition, apply pressure in waves rather than constant maximum squeeze - this prevents muscle fatigue and maintains finishing power. Use micro-adjustments between pressure waves to optimize angle. If opponent defends for more than 15 seconds, transition to rear naked choke since their hands are occupied, then immediately return to triangle when they move hands to defend the choke. This chain attacking exhausts their defensive resources systematically. Time your maximum pressure application for when they exhale or when you feel their frame weaken.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the finishing mechanism change when transitioning from rear triangle to mounted triangle mid-submission?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When opponent rotates toward you forcing a mounted triangle transition, the finish mechanics shift significantly. In mounted triangle, your weight becomes the primary control element rather than hip extension. The squeeze angle changes from perpendicular to more aligned with their spine. Adjust by sitting upright on the mount, using gravity and hip pressure rather than hip extension. The head control with your choking arm becomes less critical as mount position provides the necessary angle. Finish by squeezing knees together while settling your weight onto their chest.

knowledge_assessment.question: What safety protocols apply specifically to training the triangle from back with less experienced partners?
knowledge_assessment.answer: With less experienced partners: explain tap signals thoroughly before drilling, use only 30-40% maximum pressure intensity, release immediately at any tap without requiring multiple signals, watch for face color changes they may not recognize themselves, maintain constant verbal communication asking about pressure level, position their hands where they can easily tap your leg, and never hold the locked position for more than 5 seconds without checking in. Their unfamiliarity with blood choke sensations means they may not recognize submission danger until too late.

knowledge_assessment.question: When your triangle is locked but opponent is managing to breathe and defend, what micro-adjustments optimize the finish without requiring additional energy?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Micro-adjustments for optimization: rotate your shin slightly to ensure the bony part (not the calf muscle) contacts their carotid, slide your locking leg ankle deeper behind your knee to tighten the figure-four, pull your knees fractionally closer together, extend your hips incrementally to reduce the angle, pull opponent's chin toward their chest with your choking arm to reduce neck space. Each small adjustment compounds the pressure without significant energy expenditure. Often a 1-2 inch hip extension is the difference between defended and finished.
